text.p: The following are the main stories from Friday morning's German newspapers:

- Waigel and Tietmeyer reach agreement, currency reserves will be revalued to "levels closer to market prices". The amount to be transferred from Bundesbank to government still open. Both Waigel and Tietmeyer call it a "good" agreement. It was also still unclear at what level the Bundesbank would revalue its reserves.

- Smaller Treuhand successor BvS will finish off Treuhand work. Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt and economics ministers from eastern Germany agree to continue BvS agency beyond the end of 1998, but with a considerably smaller staff.

- Ifo institute puts forth forecast that Germany will miss the Maastricht deficit criteria in 1997 with a budget deficit amounting to 3.2 percent of GDP. The total deficit will be 120 billion marks, Ifo says. But institute president Karl Heinrich Oppenlaender says Germany will not be denied entry into EMU because the Maastricht Treaty allows certain deviations from threshold criteria.

- Waigel and Tietmeyer reach agreement on dispute over revaluation of German gold and currency reserves. The currency reserves should be revalued to a level "closer to market prices" for 1997. The profit resulting from that should go to the government in 1998. The gold reserves should not take place until 1999.

- Coalition in dispute over plans to cut the solidarity tax in 1998. Christian Democrats criticising the FDP insistence that solidarity tax be cut as planned by two points to 5.5 percent in 1998. CDU wants reduction by just one point. FDP says it will stick to the two point reduction.
- German government considering changing shareholder laws to allow companies to issue shares in the furture without a nominal value.

- Tietmeyer triumphs in dispute with Waigel. Gold reserves will not be touched for time being. Bundesbank will revalue currency reserves. Billions in profit won't reach Bonn budget until 1998 at the earliest.
- Asylum-seekers who arrived in Germany after May 15 will no longer be allowed to obtain a work permit in Germany.

- The percentage of foreigners living in Germany rose to 8.9 percent in 1996 from 8.8 percent in 1995, the statistics office says. There are about 7.31 million foreigners living in Germany, up from 7.17 million at the end of 1995. The largest group is from Turkey with two million and 1.8 million are from EU countries.
- Ifo institute raises doubts that Germany will meet the Maastricht deficit criteria.
- FDP wants to allow controlled use of heroin in a way that would help drug addicts reduce their dependencies.
